items.topic: Borderline personality disorder — DBT as gold-standard psychotherapy
items.stem: A client with borderline personality disorder asks which psychotherapy approach is considered the gold standard for this diagnosis. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), which teaches skills such as mindfulness and distress tolerance
Benzodiazepines alone are first-line and replace the need for any psychotherapy
Only electroconvulsive therapy is effective for borderline personality disorder
No psychotherapy helps; medication cures the core personality pattern

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: DBT was created for BPD and is considered the gold standard; skills include mindfulness, distress tolerance, interpersonal effectiveness, and emotion regulation. Merck: psychotherapy is the mainstay; CBT approaches include dialectical behavioral therapy.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Merck: benzodiazepines are not recommended; psychotherapy is the mainstay.
rationales.C: Incorrect. ECT is not the gold-standard first-line treatment for BPD core features.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Psychotherapy is primary treatment; medications are adjunctive and not consistently effective for core BPD symptoms.

items.topic: NGN matrix — BPD nursing: consistent limits, de-escalation, safety
items.stem: For a hospitalized adult with borderline personality disorder who is escalating emotionally, indicate whether each nursing action is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Set clear limits early and enforce them consistently across team members
Speak in a calm voice; use active listening; avoid arguing and judgmental comments
Argue heatedly with the client to prove who is right during splitting
Assess suicide/self-harm risk and implement the safety/crisis plan as needed
Touch the agitated client without permission to force compliance

rationales.R1: Indicated. OpenStax: set limits early and enforce consistently across team; set clear consistent boundaries.
rationales.R2: Indicated. OpenStax de-escalation: calm voice, active listening, avoid arguing/judgmental comments.
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Arguing fuels escalation and is explicitly to be avoided.
rationales.R4: Indicated. OpenStax lists risk for suicide/self-mutilation; crisis intervention and safety planning are core; Merck notes suicidal gestures are common.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. OpenStax: avoid touching without permission.

items.topic: NGN cloze — DBT originated for BPD; core skill domains
items.stem: Complete the teaching about dialectical behavior therapy (DBT).

ngn.template: DBT was originally developed for {B1}. Clients learn skill domains that include {B2} and {B3} to reduce impulsive crisis responses and improve relationships.

B2.text: arguing to win every interpersonal conflict

rationales.B1a: Correct. OpenStax: DBT originally created for BPD; Merck lists dialectical behavioral therapy among effective psychotherapies.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. DBT was not developed for viral pharyngitis.
rationales.B2a: Correct. OpenStax lists mindfulness and distress tolerance among DBT strategies.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. DBT teaches skillful emotion awareness, not emotional erasure.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Interpersonal effectiveness is collaborative, not win-at-all-costs arguing.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Abrupt medication stops are unsafe teaching.
rationales.B3a: Correct. OpenStax: interpersonal effectiveness and emotion regulation are DBT skill domains.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Safety concerns should be shared with the care team.
rationales.B3d: Incorrect. Impulsive spending is a BPD risk behavior, not a skill.

items.topic: Suspected transfusion reaction — stop transfusion immediately; keep IV open with normal saline
items.stem: Five minutes after starting packed red blood cells, a client reports chills, dyspnea, and back pain. What is the nurse’s priority action?

options.text: Stop the transfusion immediately and keep the IV line open with normal saline
Increase the infusion rate to finish the unit faster before notifying anyone
Ignore symptoms for 30 minutes because reactions never occur early
Restart the same unit after a brief pause without further investigation

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: if reaction symptoms occur, stop transfusion immediately and keep IV open with normal saline; send product/samples for investigation. OpenStax Skills: immediately stop the transfusion and notify the provider.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Speeding the infusion worsens exposure during a possible hemolytic/allergic reaction.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Most reactions occur in the first 15–20 minutes; early symptoms require action.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Merck: the implicated unit should not be restarted.

rows.text: Two qualified nurses verify patient identity and product compatibility before starting

rationales.R4: Not indicated. Merck: do not restart the implicated unit.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Early bedside monitoring is required.

items.topic: NGN cloze — transfusion reaction: stop; NS keep vein open; notify
items.stem: Complete the priority actions for a suspected acute transfusion reaction.

ngn.template: The nurse should first {B1}, then {B2}, and {B3}.

B1.text: speed the infusion to empty the bag
add potassium chloride to the blood tubing
ignore symptoms until the unit finishes

B2.text: keep the IV open with normal saline
flush the blood tubing with D5W into the same set
restart the same unit without notifying anyone

B3.text: notify the provider and blood bank for investigation
discard the bag so no one can investigate
tell the client reactions are imaginary

rationales.B1a: Correct. OpenStax/Merck: stop transfusion immediately when reaction is suspected.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Do not add medications to blood tubing.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Merck: keep IV open with normal saline; OpenStax MS: disconnect blood tubing and infuse NS to keep vein open.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. D5W is not the standard keep-open fluid for transfusion reactions.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Do not restart the implicated unit.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Maintain IV access for emergency treatment.
rationales.B3a: Correct. Notify provider; send product/samples to blood bank for investigation.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Document and report the event.
rationales.B3d: Incorrect. Symptoms must be taken seriously.

items.topic: Firearm injury prevention — store unloaded and locked; secure ammunition
items.stem: A community health nurse teaches a Canadian household that keeps a non-restricted firearm. Which storage teaching is most appropriate?

options.text: Store the firearm unloaded and locked (or otherwise rendered inoperable/secured), and keep ammunition locked or not readily accessible
Leave firearms loaded and unlocked on a closet shelf because out of sight equals safe storage
Store loaded firearms under a child’s bed for quick access during play
Never use locks because locking devices always make firearms safer to leave loaded

rationales.A: Correct. RCMP: unload and lock firearms; store ammunition separately or lock it up. CDC: store unloaded and locked with ammunition secured separately; out of sight/reach is not enough.
rationales.B: Incorrect. CDC: out of sight/reach is not safe storage.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Loaded unlocked access by children is a preventable injury risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Locking devices and secure storage are recommended/required.

items.topic: Sports concussion — remove from play; no same-day return; medical clearance
items.stem: A teen athlete collides during a game and shows confusion and headache suggesting concussion. What is the most appropriate immediate guidance?

options.text: Remove the athlete from play now; do not return the same day; seek healthcare clearance before return to sport
Finish the game if the athlete says they feel fine after a water break
Return to full contact immediately to 'shake it off'
Allow same-day return whenever symptoms last less than 2 minutes

rationales.A: Correct. CDC HEADS UP: remove right away; keep out the day of injury until cleared by a healthcare provider. CPS Caring for Kids: no return until cleared by a doctor; stepwise return-to-play.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Athletes should not judge severity themselves; same-day return is unsafe.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Early return increases risk of repeat concussion.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Brief symptom duration does not authorize same-day return.

items.topic: NGN matrix — sports concussion response and return-to-play teaching
items.stem: For a youth athlete with a suspected sport-related concussion, indicate whether each teaching point is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Remove the athlete from sports participation immediately
Do not return to play on the same day as the injury
Obtain healthcare provider clearance before returning to sport
Return to full-contact play the same afternoon if the athlete feels better after 10 minutes
Ignore worsening headache, repeated vomiting, or seizure after the injury

items.topic: Noise-induced hearing loss — protect hearing at ≥85 dBA with earplugs/earmuffs
items.stem: A community nurse teaches workers about preventing noise-induced hearing loss. Which instruction is most appropriate?

options.text: Wear hearing protection (earplugs or earmuffs) during loud noise exposure around 85 dBA or higher, and reduce time near the noise when possible
Hearing protection is never needed because NIHL always reverses completely overnight
Stand closer to loud machinery so exposure time is shorter and safer
Only protect hearing after permanent deafness is already diagnosed

rationales.A: Correct. NIDCD: long/repeated exposure ≥85 dBA can cause NIHL; wear earplugs/protective devices; move away if needed. CDC/NIOSH: REL 85 dBA/8 hours; always wear hearing protection in noisy areas; reduce time in noisy areas.
rationales.B: Incorrect. NIHL can be permanent; prevention is key.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Prevention should occur before irreversible loss.

items.topic: Blood transfusion — remain at bedside first 15 minutes to detect early reactions
items.stem: A nurse starts a unit of packed red blood cells. Which action best reduces the risk of missing an early transfusion reaction?

options.text: Start slowly and remain at the bedside for the first 15 minutes while monitoring for adverse reactions
Leave immediately after hanging the blood because reactions only occur after 24 hours
Run the entire unit as an IV push within 2 minutes to minimize observation time
Skip baseline vital signs because they never change during transfusion

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Skills: start slowly; remain for first 15 minutes; most reactions occur within first 15–20 minutes. OpenStax MS reinforces immediate recognition/action for reactions.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Early reactions are common; bedside monitoring is required.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Rapid push increases risk and violates timed administration guidance.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Baseline and serial vital signs are essential for detecting reactions.

items.topic: NGN cloze — concussion: remove from play; no same-day return; medical clearance
items.stem: Complete the concussion safety teaching for coaches and parents.

ngn.template: If concussion is suspected, {B1}. The athlete should {B2} and may return to sport only after {B3}.

B1.text: remove the athlete from play right away
keep playing through dizziness to build toughness

B2.text: not return to sports the same day as the injury
return to full contact after a 5-minute rest if they insist they are fine
drive alone immediately after loss of consciousness
skip telling any adult about the hit

B3.text: clearance by a healthcare provider / doctor
winning the next game without evaluation

rationales.B1a: Correct. CDC/CPS: remove from participation immediately.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Playing through symptoms risks worsening injury.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Contact should stop, not increase.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Fluid restriction is unrelated/harmful teaching.
rationales.B2a: Correct. CDC: keep out the same day of the injury.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Athlete self-report does not authorize same-day return.
rationales.B3a: Correct. CDC healthcare clearance; CPS doctor clearance before return to sport.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Competition does not replace medical clearance.
